name: Eat the rainbow / skin nutrient diet

lead: Eat the rainbow means eating fruit and vegetables of varied colours, which carry different pigments and antioxidants, with the aim of better-looking skin and general health.

The chain: fruit and vegetables are good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids, and the idea is that these antioxidants and pigments counter oxidative stress in the skin. Carotenoid intake has been linked to skin colour. Trials of antioxidant supplements found no effect, or a small increase in mortality in vulnerable groups, and no skin studies of the colour-variety approach were found.

paras: People aim to get several colours on the plate each day, such as leafy greens, orange and red vegetables, berries and citrus, mostly as part of ordinary meals. Skin changes are reported after weeks of consistent intake.

Whole produce is generally not the concern; high-dose supplements are. The CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A. Cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids.

angle.text: Users eat varied colourful produce for its vitamins, carotenoids and antioxidants, hoping for healthier-looking skin. Carotenoid intake has been linked to skin colour, while antioxidant supplement trials showed no benefit; the colour approach itself has not been studied for skin.

lead: Eating the rainbow means eating produce in a variety of colours, such as red tomatoes, orange carrots, green leaves and purple berries, for the range of vitamins, carotenoids and other pigments they contain. In appearance-focused communities it is used as a food-based way to improve skin colour and complexion, with proponents pointing to antioxidants and carotenoid pigments that show in the skin.[1][2]

Research from the University of St Andrews, published in Evolution and Human Behavior in 2011, linked higher fruit and vegetable intake with a more golden skin tone, which the researchers attributed to carotenoids, the pigments that colour carrots and tomatoes.[2] When participants chose between skin coloured by tanning and skin coloured by carotenoids, they preferred the carotenoid tone, and lead author Ian Stephen said eating lots of fruit and vegetables was more effective than sunbathing for this.[2] A perspective article by the same group argued that appearance benefits could motivate people to eat more produce and cited preliminary work finding perceptible skin colour change after a modest six-week diet change.[3]

Wikipedia describes fruits and vegetables as good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids, and notes cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids.[1] Trials of antioxidant supplements, which differ from food, found no effect or a small increase in mortality in elderly or vulnerable groups.[1]

paras: The approach asks people to include produce of several colours in their daily diet. The colour pigments reflect different compounds: carotenoids for orange, yellow and red; chlorophyll in greens; anthocyanins in purple and blue produce.[1] Wikipedia describes fruits and vegetables as good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids.[1]

In the St Andrews research, people who ate more daily portions of produce had a warmer skin tone, which the researchers credited to carotenoids.[2] Participants asked to choose the healthiest skin colour favoured carotenoid-type colouring over tan-type colouring, and a similar preference for yellower skin appeared in an African population, suggesting it is not limited to Caucasian faces.[2] Professor David Perrett, who heads the university's Perception Lab, said it was the first study to demonstrate this in humans.[2]

The Whitehead, Ozakinci, Stephen and Perrett perspective in the American Journal of Public Health (2012) proposes using appearance as a motivator for fruit and vegetable intake and calls for randomised trials; it does not report a trial of its own.[3]

Antioxidants are the usual explanation given in skin communities for why produce is thought to help the complexion. Wikipedia's article on antioxidants reports that trials of antioxidant supplements found no effect or a small increase in mortality in elderly or vulnerable groups, and that the USDA withdrew its antioxidant food measurements in 2012, stating they were not biologically relevant to human health.[1]

The University of St Andrews study (2011) linked produce intake with skin yellowness and perceived health in observational and perception experiments;[2] a perspective article cites preliminary work on six-week diet change and skin colour.[3] No randomised trial of a rainbow diet for skin appearance was found. Related research on antioxidant supplements: the CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A, and a meta-analysis of about 230,000 patients linked some antioxidant supplements to higher mortality in high-quality trials; these studies did not examine skin and involved supplements rather than food.[1]

lore.intro: Colourful produce is discussed as a skin-supporting habit in appearance communities and in news coverage of the St Andrews work.[2]

claims.claim: Eating colourful produce gives skin a healthier glow.
Antioxidant-rich produce improves skin by protecting it from oxidative damage.

timeline.event: University of St Andrews researchers report that more fruit and vegetable intake is linked to a more golden skin tone preferred by observers.[2]
Perspective article proposes appearance-based messages to promote fruit and vegetable intake.[3]
